question: The People’s Liberation Army Strategic Support Force, in charge of Chinese military cyber, electronic and information warfare, aims to increase its cooperation with six universities1, including the Chinese Academy of Sciences, Shanghai Jiatong, Xi’an Jiatong, Beijing Ligong, Nanjing University and Harbin University.

Beijing is known for bringing outside hackers into the government fold and for its fusion between military and civilian entities. Several of these universities have already been listed by the Canadian government2 as institutions that pose the highest risk to its national security due to their direct or indirect connections with military, national defence and state security entities.

This list contains more than 100 foreign universities and institutions. Researchers seeking federal grants to study in any of the fields listed as ‘sensitive research areas3’ will need to attest that they are not working with or receiving money from any of the listed entities. 1.
Are there any cooperation or exchange programmes between these listed entities and European universities or institutions?
If so, what measures can or will the Commission take to de-risk cooperation or exchanges with the listed entities?
Does the Commission intend to follow the Canadian example and establish a similar list of highrisk foreign research institutions?
answer: 1. The Commission is well aware of the risks that could emerge from international collaborations in research and innovation (R&I) and is actively working to enhance research security in the EU’s key funding programme Horizon Europ e (4) and at the level of Member States, national funding agencies and research performing organisations.

There are entities referred to by the Honourable Member participating in projects under Horizon Europe such as in the case of the Chinese Academy of Sciences taking part in the project Ecosystem-based adaptation to enhance forest resilience (eco2adapt ) (5) focusing on increasing forest resilience or Nanjing University participating in mobility projects under Erasmus + (6).

Potential risks and applicable restrictions are taken into account when considering cooperation activities. 2. In line with the Global Approach to Research and Innovation of 2021 (7), several measures have already been implemented in Horizon Europe to enhance research security (8). 3.

Beyond Horizon Europe, and in full respect of the academic freedom and the institutional autonomy of the R&I sector, the Commission is working to raise awareness on research security and encourages due diligence processes. In 2022, the toolkit on tackling R&I foreign interference (9) was published to help research performing organisations counter threats from foreign state-actors.

As a follow-up to the European Economic Security Strategy of 2023 (10), in January 2024, the Commission proposed a Council Recommendation on enhancing research security (11) that provides guidance to ensure international cooperation remains both open and secure following the principle of ‘as open as possible, as closed as necessary’. The Council adopted the recommendation in May 2024.
